catalog_quote: Hollis 1909:156-157: "The general rule is that all syllables are accentuated alike, a slight stress being perhaps laid on the penultimate. There are, however, exceptions to this rule: 1. If the penultimate syllable of a substantive (not joined to the singular article or other part of speech) is i or u followed by a, e, or o, the accent generally rests on the antepenultimate syllable: Poiisio, work. Kesua, seed. ... 2. When the singular substantive joined to the article ends in t, the two words are spoken as one, and the article is usually lightly accentuated. All syllables are, however, frequently accentuated alike ... But when the substantive joined to the article ends in ta, to, da, or do, the accent rests on the penultimate ... 3. When the plural substantive (without the article) is the same as the singular substantive, or when a difference is made by only lengthening the last vowel,…
sweep_summary: The stress-title sweep for Nandi (nand1266) turned up exactly one bibliography item, Downing 2000 'Morphological and prosodic constraints on Kinande verbal reduplication' (Phonology 17:1-38, DOI 10.1017/s095267570000381x). Crossref and the Cambridge Core abstract confirm it is about Kinande, a Bantu language of DR Congo, not Nandi (Southern Nilotic, Kenya); it is a Glottolog mis-assignment under nand1266 (as is Mutaka 1995 'Vowel harmony in Kinande' in the same reference list) and says nothing about Nandi word stress. Paywalled; priority none. No new first-hand Nandi stress statement was read: the on-disk material from the earlier pass (Creider & Creider 1989 Google Books full-text search returns zero hits for 'stress'; Toweett 1975, Kattam 2016, Kipsang 2019 UoN theses; Hyman 2000; Dimmendaal 2012; Lodge 1995; the Pressbooks Nandi profile; archive.org full-text searches) contains no statement of Nandi word-stress placement beyond what the catalog already carries, so the catalog's deciding source (Hollis 1909:156-158, 'all syllables are accentuated alike, a slight stress being perhaps laid on the penultimate', with the modern tonal description from Creider & Creider 1989 via secondary texts) stands unchallenged; catalog_kind 'tonal' is neither confirmed nor contradicted by anything new. the natural next acquisition for a modern first-hand statement remains Creider & Creider 1989 'A Grammar of Nandi' (Buske; print only, HathiTrust catalog blocked by Cloudflare in the prior pass).,; appended there.

sources.citation: Toweett, Taaitta. 1975. Kalenjin nouns and their classification, with notes on phonology and a noun list appendix. MA thesis, University of Nairobi (Institute of African Studies), 281 pp. [Kipsigis-based 'Kaaleenychiin']. Open: erepository.uonbi.ac.ke handle 11295/42264.
sources.quote: "Vowels only have tones in Kipsigiis. There are four main tones in Kipsigiis. The shortening or lengthening of each of these tones may give an impression of another different tone. The Kipsigiis tones (over a) are: Low Tone; High Tone; High-falling Tone; Low-rising Tone (rare)." followed by a chart of disyllabic tonal combinations; nominative marked 'by tonal changes in a word' (txt line 822). No statement about word stress or accent anywhere in the thesis.
sources.locator: 'Notes on Phonology' sec. XVIII 'Tone', front-matter pp. xvii-xviii (PDF pp. 37-38); full-text grep for 'stress'/'accent' returns only English glosses in the noun list (txt lines 13442, 14640, 14933).
